summary: Executed the selected structural repair in a second disposable copy. Recipe: replace both pair expressions with one left-to-right separator scan, preserve strict nonempty-name behavior, preserve permissive empty-name and leading-equals behavior, skip pair-syntax whitespace before the value, cut the value at the first newline/carriage-return/null, then apply the existing trim and control-character checks. Differential recipe: load unpatched and patched modules in one process; for each header build a structured snapshot of key, value, path, domain, expiry, max-age, secure, http-only, same-site, and extensions; compare strict and permissive parses over about 3000 fixed and seeded-random strings. The first two differential runs exposed two real edge corrections: leading whitespace after the separator must be skipped before value termination, and the permissive leading-equals fallback must skip that whitespace too. After those corrections the corpus reached about 6000 comparisons with zero mismatches. The patched 250000-character pair fixture completed in about 0.4 ms versus the earlier five-second timeout, and scaling through 250000 characters was near-linear. A secondary sink appeared: many semicolon-separated attributes still grew superlinearly because the parser removed elements from the front of an array in a loop. About 96000 attributes took 1.4 s in the pair-patched copy, while an experimental index-iteration copy took about 14 ms with identical extension counts. Evidence is strong local regression evidence; the second repair was not yet in the final copy, and no official harness ran.
next_hint: The deterministic pair split matches the original on the differential corpus and removes the pair stall, but the attribute loop has its own front-removal cost. Decide whether merging index iteration into the same patch preserves every attribute and extension, and re-run the combined differential and scaling gates.
